note: An old puzzle about free will, discussed by Aristotle and Thomas Aquinas and later known as Buridan's ass: a creature drawn equally to two equal goods could never choose between them. Dante has two questions pulling at him with equal force, and so asks neither.
Dante's Italian says he neither blames nor praises himself. His silence was forced on him, and what is forced earns neither blame nor credit. That is the very question he wants to ask about Piccarda.

King Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon had a dream he could not recall, and in his fury ordered all his wise men killed when they could not tell him what it was. The prophet Daniel, taught by God, told him both the dream and its meaning (Daniel 2). Beatrice too reads what has not been said.
The first doubt. Piccarda and Constance were dragged from their convents. If they never stopped wanting to keep their vows, why should it count against them?

context: The second doubt. Plato taught that each soul comes down from a star and goes back to it after death. Meeting souls in the moon seems to prove him right.

note: The question about Plato is the dangerous one, because it touches doctrine. The Church taught that God creates each soul directly for its body. It does not come down from a star.

context: The Seraphim are the highest of the nine orders, the nearest to God.

note: The prophet and last judge of Israel, who anointed its first kings, Saul and David.
John the Baptist, who baptized Christ, or John the apostle and evangelist.

context: Named last as the highest of all: not even she has her seat in a different heaven from Piccarda's.

note: Plato gave souls longer or shorter stays among the stars. All the blessed have the same eternity.

context: The key to reading the Paradiso. Every blessed soul lives here. The planets below are a stage on which they show themselves to Dante, each group in the sphere that matches its degree of bliss.

note: The Spirit of God. The blessed differ only in how much of it each can take in.
A principle from Aristotle: nothing reaches the mind except by way of the senses. So Heaven turns spiritual truths into things Dante can see. The line also describes how his own poem works.
The Bible speaks of God's hand, his arm, his footstool. God has no body: these are figures suited to human readers.
Two archangels. Gabriel announced the birth of Christ to Mary, and Michael leads the armies of Heaven against Satan. Angels have no bodies, but painters give them human shape.
The archangel Raphael. In the Book of Tobit he travels in disguise with the young Tobias and cures his father's blindness. In the Latin Bible father and son are both called Tobias.
Plato's dialogue on the making of the universe, named for its main speaker. It was the one work of Plato widely read in the medieval West, in a partial Latin translation.
Plato seems to mean it literally. The souls in the moon are only a sign, so the two cases are not alike.

Beatrice offers Plato a kinder reading. If he meant only that the stars shape human character, he is partly right. Dante held that the heavens incline people one way or another but never force the will (Purgatorio 16).
The pagans felt the power of the planets, took them for gods and prayed to them. The planets still carry the gods' names.
Beatrice speaks here as the voice of revealed truth. The second doubt, unlike the first, cannot draw Dante into heresy.
Dante's phrase is usually read as "evidence of faith". To be troubled that God's justice looks unjust, one must already believe that God is just.
Aristotle's definition in the Ethics: an act is forced only when the person it is done to contributes nothing to it.

quote: Will is never extinguished unless it wills to be
note: The heart of the answer. No outside force can make the will consent. It is like a flame, which springs upright again however often it is blown aside.
Once the men who seized them were gone, they could have gone back to the convent, at whatever cost. They did not, and to that extent they went along with the force.
Saint Lawrence, a deacon of the church of Rome, martyred in 258. By tradition he was roasted on an iron grill, and told his torturers to turn him over because one side was done.

Gaius Mucius Scaevola, a hero of early Rome. Captured after failing to kill the enemy king Porsenna, he held his right hand in a fire until it burned away, to show how little Romans feared pain (Livy, book 2).
Beatrice is still speaking, and goes on to the end of her answer.
She said so in Canto 3: the light that gives these souls peace will not let them stray from the truth.

context: Piccarda said Constance never put off the veil in her heart. Beatrice has just said that both women gave in. One of them seems to be wrong.

note: His father, the seer Amphiaraus, was sent to his death in the war against Thebes by his wife Eriphyle, who had been bribed with a necklace. He charged his son to avenge him, and Alcmaeon killed his mother. The play on dutiful and pitiless comes from Ovid's Metamorphoses (book 9).

A distinction from the schools. The absolute will is what a person wants in itself. The other will is what the person actually chooses in the circumstances, as a sailor in a storm chooses to throw his cargo overboard. Constance never wanted to leave the veil, yet out of fear she chose to stay in the world.
Beatrice's speech. Its source, the fountain of all truth, is God.
Beatrice, loved by God.
God, the truth that holds every other truth. Nothing less will satisfy the human mind.

quote: every desire would end in failure
note: An argument from Aristotle: nature gives no desire in vain. The mind hungers for the whole truth, so the whole truth must be within its reach.

quote: doubt springs up like a green shoot
note: Each truth learned raises a new question. Doubt is not the enemy of truth here but its offshoot, and it drives the mind upward.
The third question, answered in Canto 5: can a broken vow be made good by some other good work? "You" is plural in the Italian: the court of Heaven.
